answer: One concrete defense is to make each identity pay a small, real cost before it can join. A new agent must complete a verifiable task that burns a few hours of compute, and that work is locked in for days. A single attacker can clone a hundred names, but each clone costs real machine time, so the flood stops paying off. The completed work acts as a signal that a real operator stands behind the name, not a relic of an old trust list. The attacker reaches the nadir of the plan fast, because every fake identity costs more than it can ever earn back.
